blocks.text: "This woman has painful antepartum vaginal bleeding associated with significant uterine tenderness and hypertonicity. The clinical picture is highly suggestive of placental abruption. I am concerned about concealed haemorrhage and maternal and fetal compromise. I would urgently assess and stabilise the mother, obtain blood investigations including FBC, coagulation and fibrinogen, crossmatch blood, assess fetal wellbeing with CTG, and involve the senior obstetric and anaesthetic teams. The need for urgent delivery would depend on maternal and fetal status."

"This woman has severe abdominal pain, a tense tender uterus and maternal tachycardia with minimal visible vaginal bleeding. I am highly concerned about concealed placental abruption. The visible blood loss may underestimate the true haemorrhage. I would initiate urgent maternal resuscitation, assess for coagulopathy, crossmatch blood, assess fetal wellbeing and arrange delivery based on maternal and fetal condition."

"This woman has clinical features of placental abruption complicated by intrauterine fetal death. My immediate priority is maternal stabilisation and assessment for haemorrhage and DIC. I would obtain urgent FBC, coagulation studies and fibrinogen, arrange blood products as required, involve senior obstetric and anaesthetic teams and plan vaginal delivery where feasible, while continuing close maternal monitoring."

"I would treat this as suspected placental abruption and first assess maternal stability using an ABCDE approach. I would call for senior obstetric and anaesthetic assistance, establish two large-bore IV accesses if significantly bleeding, send FBC, group and crossmatch, coagulation studies including fibrinogen, and renal function, and activate the major obstetric haemorrhage protocol if indicated. I would assess fetal wellbeing with CTG and remember that the amount of visible bleeding may underestimate concealed haemorrhage. Ultrasound may support the diagnosis but a normal scan does not exclude abruption. I would carefully manage fluids, administer blood products and correct coagulopathy as required. If the fetus is alive with persistent compromise or the mother is deteriorating, I would arrange urgent delivery after maternal stabilisation. If there is intrauterine fetal death and the mother is stable, vaginal delivery is generally preferred. I would also monitor closely for DIC, acute kidney injury and postpartum haemorrhage."
